profile.address: Meridian Parkway, Meridian Business Campus, Aurora, Naperville Township, DuPage County, Illinois, 60598
profile.reading:
This building at 4267 Meridian Parkway in Aurora, Illinois -- tagged in this record under the name "Lincoln Rackhouse" -- has changed hands since that name was attached to it. The roughly 70,000-square-foot facility, with about 33,000 square feet of technical white space, was originally built around 2007 for CNA Insurance's own data processing needs before being converted to a multi-tenant data center. It later passed through ownership by Bytegrid and Lincoln Rackhouse, a data-center investment and operating platform, before being acquired by Michigan-based colocation and cloud provider US Signal, as reported by trade press covering the deal. At acquisition, the facility was reported to have about 1.35 megawatts of IT capacity in active use against a planned build-out toward 4 megawatts of critical capacity (roughly 6 megawatts of commercial/utility power), giving US Signal substantial room to grow into the space as demand increased.

Lincoln Rackhouse itself was a real estate and data-center operating arm associated with Lincoln Property Company, one of the larger private real estate investment and development firms in the United States, active in acquiring and repositioning data center assets for institutional ownership. Its presence in this building's history reflects a common pattern in the data center industry: purpose-built or converted facilities frequently change operators and brands as investment platforms buy, reposition, and resell them to operating companies better positioned to fill them with tenants.

For prospective and current customers, the facility today functions as a Chicago-area colocation site for US Signal rather than as an active Lincoln Rackhouse property, and readers should not expect to find current marketing, pricing, or capacity information under the Lincoln Rackhouse name. The Aurora location places it in the western Chicago suburbs, within reach of the Chicago metro's substantial enterprise and financial-services customer base while avoiding the highest real estate costs of the city core. No additional zoning, permit, or expansion filings specific to the post-acquisition period under US Signal were identified in public reporting. US Signal, the current operator, is a Michigan-based provider of colocation, cloud, and network services aimed primarily at midwestern enterprise and public-sector customers, and the Aurora building fits a pattern common to that segment of the industry: rather than building new facilities from the ground up, regional colocation providers frequently expand their geographic footprint by acquiring existing, already-powered buildings with room to grow, since the electrical infrastructure, generator plant, and physical security systems already in place represent most of a data center's upfront cost and lead time. That the site was originally built for a single insurance company's internal computing needs before being converted for multi-tenant use is itself a common origin story in the industry -- many of the colocation facilities operating today began as corporate-owned data centers that were later repurposed once their original occupants outgrew them, consolidated elsewhere, or moved workloads to the cloud.

reading.body:
This facility has no published power specifications, so its scale relative to Illinois data center capacity cannot be determined from operator disclosures. Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities, but only six publish power figures totaling 236 MW, making Lincoln Rackhouse one of many sites in the state with no disclosed capacity.

The research note provided describes Lincoln Rackhouse as the data center division of Lincoln Property Company, a real estate services firm, rather than a pure-play operator. The note documents the division's formation in 2010 and its business model combining property ownership, tenant representation, and facilities management, but contains no specifications for this specific DuPage County facility.

Without published power consumption, IT load capacity, or cooling specifications, this campus cannot be assessed for its relevance to AI scaling. The ranking as seventh by published megawatts appears to reflect missing data rather than actual capacity, since no megawatts are published for this site.
